subject: anatomy
title: Lower Limb Neurovascular Pathology: Peroneal Nerve, Venous System, and Varicosities

steps.tx: The common peroneal nerve (L4-S2) is the smaller terminal division of the sciatic nerve. Descending along the medial border of the biceps femoris tendon, it winds directly around the subcutaneously situated **neck of the fibula**, entering the lateral compartment by piercing the substance of the peroneus longus muscle.
steps.say: The common peroneal nerve is the smaller branch of the sciatic nerve. Winding around the subcutaneous neck of the fibula, it passes through peroneus longus to divide into superficial and deep branches.

vis.alt: Common peroneal nerve winding around the neck of the fibula and its bifurcation into deep and superficial branches
vis.caption: Course of the common peroneal nerve winding around the neck of the fibula. [Credit: StewardMD]

steps.tx: Its superficial position against the hard periosteum of the fibular neck renders the common peroneal nerve the most frequently injured nerve in the lower extremity. Direct trauma, tight plaster casts, or fibular fractures cause nerve palsy manifesting with flaccid **foot drop** and sensory loss over the dorsum of the foot and lateral leg.
steps.say: Its superficial location against the fibular neck makes the common peroneal nerve exceptionally vulnerable. Direct blows or tight leg casts cause foot drop and sensory loss over the foot dorsum.

left.title: Motor Deficits in Foot Drop
points: Paralysis of tibialis anterior: loss of dorsiflexion
Paralysis of peroneus longus/brevis: loss of eversion
Paralysis of EDL and EHL: loss of toe extension
High-stepping gait to avoid dragging toes

right.title: Sensory Deficits in Foot Drop
points: Loss over lower two-thirds of lateral leg
Loss across broad expanse of foot dorsum
Loss in first dorsal web space (deep branch)

steps.tx: The venous drainage of the lower limb is divided into superficial and deep systems connected by communicating perforating veins. The **great saphenous vein** originates from the medial end of the dorsal venous arch, ascends anterior to the medial malleolus, travels along the medial knee, and pierces the cribriform fascia at the saphenous opening.
steps.say: Superficial veins connect to deep veins through perforating vessels. The great saphenous vein begins on the medial foot, ascends anterior to the medial malleolus, and enters the femoral vein at the saphenous opening.

vis.title: Ascending Trajectory of Great Saphenous Vein

steps.tx: Incompetence of valves within the saphenous trunks or perforating veins causes retrograde hydrostatic hypertension, transforming straight veins into dilated, tortuous **varicose veins**. Chronic venous hypertension leads to skin lipodermatosclerosis, stasis eczema, and non-healing venous ulcers characteristically localized over the medial gaiter area.
steps.say: Valvular incompetence in saphenous trunks or perforator veins causes retrograde hydrostatic hypertension, creating varicose veins. Chronic stasis yields skin induration, eczema, and medial gaiter ulcers.

vis.alt: Stripped long saphenous vein specimen displaying marked tortuosity and nodular varicosities
vis.caption: Surgically stripped varicose great saphenous vein demonstrating valvular failure and saccular dilatation. [Credit: StewardMD]

steps.tx: Clinical assessment of valvular competence uses the **Trendelenburg test** for varicose veins. With the patient supine and the limb elevated to empty the veins, a tourniquet is applied at the upper thigh: rapid retrograde filling upon standing before tourniquet release confirms saphenofemoral junction incompetence, while sudden filling upon release proves trunk valve failure.
steps.say: The Trendelenburg test evaluates venous valve competence. With the leg elevated and a tourniquet applied at the groin, rapid filling upon standing identifies saphenofemoral junction incompetence.

rows: Patent deep veins with competent pump

steps.tx: The small saphenous vein arises from the lateral dorsal venous arch, ascends posterior to the **lateral malleolus** alongside the sural nerve, and pierces the deep popliteal fascia to drain into the popliteal vein. The sural nerve provides sensory innervation to the lateral margin of the foot and little toe.
steps.say: The small saphenous vein ascends behind the lateral malleolus with the sural nerve, draining into the popliteal vein. The sural nerve supplies cutaneous sensation to the lateral foot border and little toe.

left.title: Great Saphenous Vein
points: Accompanied by saphenous nerve in leg
Drains into femoral vein at saphenous opening

right.title: Small Saphenous Vein
points: Accompanied by sural nerve in calf
Drains into popliteal vein in popliteal fossa

steps.tx: Entrapment of the lateral femoral cutaneous nerve (L2, L3) beneath the lateral attachment of the inguinal ligament near the ASIS causes **meralgia paraesthetica**. Characterized by burning pain, paresthesias, and hypersensitivity over the anterolateral thigh, it occurs frequently in pregnancy, obesity, or with tight utility belts.
steps.say: Entrapment of the lateral femoral cutaneous nerve under the inguinal ligament causes meralgia paraesthetica. It produces burning pain and tingling over the anterolateral thigh without any motor loss.

steps.tx: Superficial **inguinal lymph nodes** are arranged in a T-shaped configuration below the inguinal ligament. The horizontal group drains the anterior abdominal wall below the umbilicus, external genitalia (excluding testes), perineum, and anal canal below the pectinate line, while the vertical group along the great saphenous vein drains the superficial lower limb.
steps.say: Superficial inguinal lymph nodes form a T-shaped cluster. The horizontal chain drains the infraumbilical abdominal wall, external genitalia, and perineum, while the vertical chain drains the lower limb.
